front: State pseudo-transitivity.
back: If X -> Y and WY -> Z, then WX -> Z; it is derived from augmentation and transitivity.

front: What is a canonical cover?
back: A minimal set of FDs equivalent to F with no extraneous attributes and no redundant dependencies.

front: What is a deletion anomaly?
back: Deleting one fact unintentionally removes another, such as losing a department's head when its last student row is deleted.

front: How can a relation be in 3NF but not in BCNF?
back: When a non-superkey determinant determines a prime attribute, e.g. teacher -> subject where subject is part of a candidate key.

front: Which property may be lost when decomposing to BCNF?
back: Dependency preservation; a BCNF decomposition is always lossless but some FDs may need a join to check.

front: Name the four SQL sub-languages with one command each.
back: DDL (CREATE), DML (INSERT), DCL (GRANT) and TCL (COMMIT).

front: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
back: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates.

front: When is a view usually updatable?
back: When it is defined on one base table without aggregates, GROUP BY, DISTINCT or set operations and includes all required NOT NULL columns.

front: What is an assertion in SQL?
back: A named schema-level condition, written CREATE ASSERTION ... CHECK (...), that the database must satisfy at all times.

front: Which relational algebra operators are fundamental?
back: Selection, projection, rename, union, set difference and Cartesian product; join, intersection and division are derived.

front: Why push selections down in a query tree?
back: Filtering rows early shrinks intermediate results, so later joins process fewer tuples and blocks.

front: What are the main steps of query processing?
back: Parsing and translation, optimization, and evaluation of the chosen execution plan.

front: What are the two phases of two-phase locking?
back: Growing phase, in which locks are acquired but none released, then shrinking phase, in which locks are released but none acquired.

front: How does strict 2PL differ from rigorous 2PL?
back: Strict 2PL holds only exclusive locks until commit or abort; rigorous 2PL holds all locks, shared and exclusive, until commit or abort.

front: In a wait-for graph, what does an edge Ti -> Tj mean?
back: Transaction Ti is waiting for a lock that Tj currently holds.

front: Why do wait-die and wound-wait not cause starvation?
back: A rolled-back transaction restarts with its original timestamp, so it eventually becomes the oldest and is never rolled back again.

front: What does the log record <Ti, X, V1, V2> store?
back: That Ti wrote item X, changing it from old value V1 (used for undo) to new value V2 (used for redo).

front: Why does deferred modification never need undo?
back: The database is written only after the transaction partially commits, so an incomplete transaction has changed nothing on disk.

front: What three steps does a checkpoint perform?
back: Flush all log records in memory to stable storage, flush all modified buffer blocks to disk, then write a <checkpoint L> record to stable storage.

front: How does shadow paging commit a transaction?
back: By atomically switching the single on-disk pointer from the shadow page table to the current page table.

front: What does fork() return in parent and child?
back: It returns the child's PID (> 0) in the parent, 0 in the child, and -1 if creation failed.

front: What is the convoy effect?
back: In FCFS, short processes wait behind one long CPU-bound process, lowering CPU and device utilisation.

front: What does a thread have privately, and what does it share?
back: Private: thread ID, program counter, registers and stack. Shared with sibling threads: code, data, heap and open files.

front: How is starvation in priority scheduling prevented?
back: By ageing: gradually increasing the priority of processes that have waited a long time.

front: State the three requirements of a critical-section solution.
back: Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

front: What shared variables does Peterson's solution use?
back: A boolean array flag[2] showing interest and an integer turn showing whose turn it is to defer.

front: Name the four Coffman conditions for deadlock.
back: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait; all four must hold simultaneously.

front: How does monitor signal differ from semaphore signal?
back: x.signal() has no effect if no process is waiting, whereas semaphore V always increments the value and is remembered.

front: Initial values of the semaphores in the bounded-buffer solution?
back: mutex = 1, empty = n (number of slots), full = 0.

front: Who can starve in the first readers-writers solution?
back: Writers, because a continuous stream of readers keeps read_count above zero and rw_mutex locked.

front: Name two ways to prevent deadlock in dining philosophers.
back: Allow at most four philosophers to sit at once, or use asymmetric pick-up (odd take left first, even take right first); a monitor that picks up both chopsticks together also works.

front: What is a safe state?
back: A state in which there is at least one order (safe sequence) in which all processes can obtain their maximum needs and finish.

front: What happens on a page fault, in brief?
back: The OS traps, finds a free or victim frame, reads the page from disk, updates the page table and restarts the faulting instruction.

front: Why are OPT and LRU immune to Belady's anomaly?
back: They are stack algorithms: the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1 frames.

front: What is thrashing and how does the working-set model prevent it?
back: Thrashing is excessive paging with little useful work; the OS suspends processes when the total working-set size exceeds available frames.

front: 32-bit virtual address, 4 KB pages, 4-byte entries: page-table size?
Absolute vs relative path?
back: An absolute path starts from the root (/home/ram/a.txt); a relative path starts from the current working directory (a.txt or ../ram/a.txt).

front: What does the superblock contain?
back: Volume-wide information: block size, number of blocks and inodes, and free-block and free-inode counts and pointers.

front: Why is an acyclic-graph directory preferred to a general graph?
back: It allows sharing via links while forbidding cycles, so traversal and deletion stay simple without garbage collection.

front: Which allocation method suffers most from external fragmentation?
back: Contiguous allocation, because each file needs one run of free blocks and deletions leave scattered holes.

front: How does C-SCAN differ from SCAN?
back: C-SCAN services requests in one direction only and then returns to the start without servicing, giving more uniform waiting times.

front: What is a FAT?
back: A file allocation table: linked allocation where the next-block pointers are held in one table at the start of the volume rather than inside each block.

front: Why does journaling speed up crash recovery?
back: Metadata changes are first logged as transactions, so after a crash only the log is replayed instead of checking the whole file system.

front: What permissions does chmod 750 set?
back: rwxr-x---: owner read/write/execute, group read/execute, others no access.

front: Which Linux process has PID 1 and what does it do?
back: init or, on modern systems, systemd; it starts services and brings the system to the default run level or target.

front: Graceful vs forced shutdown?
back: Graceful warns users, stops processes and services, syncs and unmounts file systems; forced skips this and risks data loss and file-system inconsistency.

front: Which sorting algorithms run in O(n log n) in the worst case?
back: Merge sort and heap sort (quick sort is O(n²) in the worst case).

front: State the four Coffman conditions for deadlock.
back: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait; all four must hold for deadlock.

front: What makes a relation BCNF but not just 3NF?
back: In BCNF every determinant of a non-trivial FD is a superkey; 3NF also allows X → A when A is a prime attribute.

front: What is the difference between an ADT and a data structure?
back: An ADT specifies the data and operations logically without implementation; a data structure is a concrete memory implementation of it, e.g. Stack ADT implemented by an array.

front: How many times does for (i = n; i > 1; i /= 2) execute?
back: About log2 n times, so the loop is O(log n).

front: State the tight bound of f(n) = 3n² + 5n + 2.
back: Θ(n²): it is O(n²) with c = 4, n0 = 6 and Ω(n²) with c = 3.

front: What does the master theorem give for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n?
back: a = 2, b = 2, d = 1 = log2 2, so T(n) = Θ(n log n).

front: What is the difference between internal and external sorting?
back: Internal sorting keeps all records in main memory; external sorting handles files too large for memory by sorting chunks and merging them from disk.

front: Which simple sort makes the fewest swaps, and how many?
back: Selection sort, at most n - 1 swaps, though it always makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons.

front: What does the partition step of quick sort guarantee?
back: The pivot ends in its final sorted position with all smaller-or-equal keys on its left and larger keys on its right.

front: Which of insertion, selection and bubble sort are stable?
back: Insertion and bubble sort are stable; selection sort is not because its long swaps can reorder equal keys.

front: What is the difference between a schema and an instance?
back: The schema is the logical design of the database and rarely changes; the instance is the data stored at a given moment and changes with every update.

front: What is a partial key (discriminator)?
back: The attribute set that distinguishes weak entities belonging to the same owner; combined with the owner's key it forms the weak entity's primary key.

front: Which kind of data independence is harder to achieve, and why?
back: Logical data independence, because application programs and views depend heavily on the logical structure of tables and attributes.

front: Name the five transaction states.
back: Active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted; committed and aborted are the terminal states.

front: When do two operations in a schedule conflict?
back: When they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write.

front: What is a cascadeless schedule?
back: One in which every transaction reads only data written by already-committed transactions, so an abort never forces other transactions to roll back.

front: Which SQL isolation level prevents dirty and unrepeatable reads but still allows phantoms?
back: Repeatable Read.

front: What runs inside a microkernel, and what runs outside it?
back: Only minimal services run in the kernel: IPC, basic scheduling and low-level memory management. File systems, device drivers and networking run as user-space servers.

front: Difference between an interrupt and a trap?
back: An interrupt is an asynchronous hardware signal from a device or timer; a trap is a synchronous software event such as a system call or an exception like divide by zero.

front: Hard vs soft real-time OS?
back: Hard real-time guarantees every deadline is met (missing one is a failure); soft real-time gives critical tasks priority but tolerates occasional deadline misses.

front: Which system-call category do fork, exec and wait belong to?
back: Process control.

front: Which address-binding time allows a process to be moved in memory while it runs?
back: Execution-time binding, where the MMU translates each logical address at run time using a relocation register or page table.

front: Internal vs external fragmentation?
back: Internal is wasted space inside an allocated block (fixed partitions, last page); external is free memory split into holes too small to use (variable partitions, segmentation).

front: What is the main drawback of best fit?
back: It must search the entire hole list (unless sorted) and leaves many tiny leftover holes that are too small to reuse.

front: Page size 1 KB, logical address 3085, page 3 in frame 7: physical address?
What are the four quadrants of each loop in Boehm's spiral model?
back: Determine objectives, alternatives and constraints; evaluate alternatives and resolve risks; develop and verify the product; plan the next iteration.

front: Name the three Scrum artefacts and the five Scrum events.
back: Artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, increment. Events: the sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review and sprint retrospective.

front: Throwaway vs evolutionary prototype?
back: A throwaway prototype is discarded once it has clarified requirements; an evolutionary prototype is refined step by step into the delivered system.

front: When is the Big Bang model acceptable?
back: Only for very small, academic or experimental projects with one or two developers, where the lack of planning carries little risk.

front: What distinguishes upper, lower and integrated CASE?
back: Upper CASE supports requirements and design, lower CASE supports coding, testing and maintenance, and I-CASE supports the whole life cycle through one repository.

front: What is the CASE repository?
back: The central database (data dictionary or encyclopedia) holding all project artefacts and their relationships, shared by every tool in an I-CASE environment.

front: Define round-trip engineering.
back: Keeping design models and source code synchronised, so changes in the code update the model and changes in the model regenerate the code.

front: What are Sommerville's three classes of non-functional requirement?
back: Product requirements, organisational requirements and external requirements (regulatory, ethical and legislative).

front: What is a domain requirement?
back: A requirement derived from the application domain, such as a standard formula or industry rule, rather than from a specific user's needs.

front: Which three types of interface must be specified in the requirements?
back: Procedural interfaces (APIs), data structures passed between subsystems, and representations of data such as bit ordering.

front: User requirements vs system requirements?
back: User requirements are abstract natural-language statements for customers; system requirements are detailed, precise specifications for developers and can form part of the contract.

front: What are the three main sections of an IEEE 830 SRS?
back: 1 Introduction, 2 Overall description, and 3 Specific requirements, followed by appendices and an index.

front: List the five requirements validation checks.
back: Validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability.

front: Forward vs backward traceability?
back: Backward traceability links a requirement to its source stakeholder or document; forward traceability links it to the design elements, code and tests that implement it.

front: What does TELOS stand for in a feasibility study?
back: Technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.

front: What are the two centralised and two event-based control models?
back: Centralised: call–return and manager models. Event-based: broadcast and interrupt-driven models.

front: In the manager control model, what does the manager do?
back: One system component acts as manager that starts, stops and coordinates the other concurrent processes, often by polling state in a loop.

front: What is a reference architecture?
back: An idealised, domain-level architecture such as the OSI model, used as a standard to compare and evaluate real system designs rather than to be implemented directly.

front: What is the role of an Object Request Broker (ORB)?
back: It is middleware that locates remote objects, marshals and transmits requests and parameters, and returns results, so objects can communicate transparently across the network.

front: Why is an ATM network a typical fat-client system?
back: Each ATM performs application processing locally and the central server only manages the account database, so the client carries both presentation and logic.

front: Name the three classic web-service standards and their roles.
back: SOAP for message exchange, WSDL for describing the service interface, and UDDI for discovering services.

front: List the main components of a real-time operating system.
back: Real-time clock, interrupt handler, scheduler, resource manager and dispatcher, with configuration and fault managers in larger systems.

front: Differentiate periodic and aperiodic stimuli.
back: Periodic stimuli occur at predictable time intervals (e.g. sensor polled every 50 ms); aperiodic stimuli occur irregularly and are usually signalled by interrupts.

front: What are the three types of component composition?
back: Sequential (glue code calls components in turn), hierarchical (one component calls another's provided services) and additive (interfaces combined into a new component).

front: Name three kinds of interface incompatibility in component composition.
back: Parameter incompatibility, operation incompatibility and operation incompleteness; they are resolved by writing adaptor components.

front: What does cyclomatic complexity tell a tester?
back: It is the number of linearly independent paths in the flow graph, i.e. the upper bound on tests needed to cover every statement and branch in basis path testing.

front: Input valid range is 18 to 60. Give the standard BVA test values.
back: 18, 19, a nominal value such as 39, 59 and 60 (5 tests = 4n + 1 for one variable); robustness adds 17 and 61.

front: What distinguishes a data-driven from a keyword-driven automation framework?
back: Data-driven keeps input and expected values in external files so one script runs many data sets; keyword-driven describes test steps as keywords in tables interpreted by the framework.

front: A module of 8 KLOC has 24 defects. What is its defect density?
back: 24 / 8 = 3 defects per KLOC.

front: Estimate effort and duration for a 32 KLOC organic project with basic COCOMO.
back: E = 2.4 x 32^1.05 = about 91 person-months; D = 2.5 x 91.3^0.38 = about 13.9 months, so roughly 6.6 people on average.

front: What are the five components counted in function point analysis?
back: External inputs, external outputs, external inquiries, internal logical files and external interface files.

front: What does Putnam's model imply about compressing the schedule?
back: Effort is proportional to 1 / td^4, so even a small reduction in delivery time requires a large increase in effort.

front: What are the four steps of statistical SQA?
back: Collect and categorise defect data, trace each defect to its root cause, use the Pareto principle to isolate the vital few causes, and correct those causes.

front: List the roles in a Fagan inspection.
back: Moderator (leads), author, reader (paraphrases the work product), recorder/scribe and inspectors.

front: What is the difference between a measure, a metric and an indicator?
back: A measure is a quantitative value of an attribute, a metric relates measures to the degree an attribute is present, and an indicator combines metrics to give insight for decisions.

front: What is a baseline in SCM?
back: A formally reviewed and agreed work product that serves as the basis for further development and can be changed only through formal change control.

front: What are Sommerville's four configuration management activities?
back: Change management, version management, system building and release management.

front: What does an engineering change order (ECO) record?
back: The approved change, the constraints to respect, and the criteria for review and audit; it is issued after the CCB approves a change request.

front: Distinguish primary, supporting and offstage actors.
back: Primary actors have goals fulfilled by the system, supporting actors provide services to it, and offstage actors have an interest in its behaviour without interacting directly.

front: What are the three use case formats?
back: Brief (one-paragraph main success scenario), casual (informal paragraphs for several scenarios) and fully dressed (all steps, variations and supporting sections).

front: What is the main success scenario and what are extensions?
back: The main success scenario is the typical happy path to the goal; extensions are all the alternative success and failure branches from its steps.

front: What does FURPS+ stand for?
back: Functional, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability, plus constraints such as implementation, interface, operations, packaging and legal.

front: Who created UML and which body standardises it?
back: The Three Amigos, Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson; it is standardised by the Object Management Group (OMG).

front: What is a domain model?
back: A visual representation of real-world conceptual classes, their associations and attributes, drawn as a UML class diagram without operations.

front: When should you add a description class such as ProductDescription?
back: When deleting the described instances would lose information, when many items share the same description, or to remove redundant data.

front: Name the three strategies for identifying conceptual classes.
back: Reuse or modify existing models, use a conceptual class category list, and noun phrase identification in use case text.

front: What is a system sequence diagram?
back: A diagram showing, for one use case scenario, the events external actors send to the system treated as a black box, in order.

front: What are the three categories of operation contract postconditions?
back: Instance creation or deletion, attribute modification, and associations formed or broken.

front: How do you decide between an attribute and a conceptual class?
back: If the concept is not thought of as a number or text in the real world, model it as a conceptual class with an association, not as an attribute.

front: Aggregation vs composition notation?
back: Aggregation is a hollow diamond (parts independent); composition is a filled diamond (parts owned and destroyed with the whole).

front: What is the difference between the alt and opt combined fragments?
back: alt has two or more guarded operands and exactly one runs (if-else); opt has a single operand that runs only if its guard is true (if with no else).

front: How is message order shown in a communication diagram?
back: By sequence numbers on the messages, with nested Dewey-decimal numbers (1, 1.1, 1.2) showing calls made while handling an earlier message.

front: What does an activation bar on a lifeline mean?
back: The period during which that object is executing an operation, either directly or through operations it has called.

front: How is object destruction shown in a sequence diagram?
back: With a large X at the bottom of the object's lifeline, typically after a <<destroy>> message.

front: What does the GRASP Information Expert pattern say?
back: Assign a responsibility to the class that has the information needed to fulfil it, e.g. Sale computes its own total because it knows its line items.

front: When does GRASP Creator say class B should create instances of A?
back: When B contains or aggregates A, records A, closely uses A, or has the initialising data for A.

front: What is Pure Fabrication?
back: A made-up class that does not represent a domain concept, created to achieve high cohesion and low coupling, such as a PersistentStorage or Factory class.

front: Which GoF pattern provides one simplified interface to a complex subsystem?
back: Facade, a structural pattern that places a single front object before a set of subsystem classes.

front: Name the four kinds of visibility between objects.
back: Attribute (B is a field of A), parameter (B passed to A's method), local (B is a local variable in A's method) and global (B is globally reachable, e.g. Singleton).

front: What does a navigability arrow from Register to Sale mean in a DCD?
back: Register holds a reference (attribute visibility) to Sale and can send it messages; Sale does not necessarily know Register.

front: What does the UML visibility marker ~ mean?
back: Package visibility: the member is accessible to any class in the same package.

front: What does a DCD add that a domain model does not have?
back: Method signatures, full attribute types and visibility, navigability arrows, dependencies, interfaces and software-only classes.

front: How is a navigable association with multiplicity * implemented in code?
back: As a collection attribute (e.g. List<SalesLineItem> or Map<ItemID, ProductDescription>) in the source class.

front: What does a create message in a sequence diagram become in code?
back: A constructor call using new; the message's parameters define the constructor's parameters.

front: Where do the statements inside a method body come from?
back: From the messages the receiving object sends in the interaction diagram, taken in sequence-number order.

front: How is interface realisation written in Java and in C++?
back: Java uses 'class X implements I'; C++ derives the class from an abstract base class containing pure virtual functions.

front: What is the difference between a checked and an unchecked exception in Java?
back: A checked exception must be caught or declared with throws, enforced at compile time; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) are not enforced.

front: How does an Error differ from an Exception in Java?
back: Error signals serious system problems such as OutOfMemoryError that applications should not normally catch; Exception covers recoverable conditions.

front: What happens when a method does not catch an exception it raises?
back: It propagates up the call stack to successive callers until a matching catch is found; if none is found the thread terminates with a stack trace.

front: How do you create a custom checked exception in Java?
back: Define a class that extends Exception (extend RuntimeException instead for an unchecked one), usually passing a message to super().

front: Order the types of coupling from best to worst.
back: Data, stamp, control, external, common, content coupling.

front: Name the five CMMI maturity levels in order.
back: Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing.

front: What do the UML visibility markers +, −, # and ~ mean?
back: Public, private, protected and package visibility.

front: What is the difference between a stub and a driver?
back: A stub stands in for a module that the unit under test calls (top-down integration); a driver calls the unit under test (bottom-up integration).

front: Why does software deteriorate even though it does not wear out?
back: Each change made during maintenance can introduce new defects (side effects), so the minimum failure rate slowly rises over the system's life.

front: Name McCall's three quality perspectives and the factors in product revision.
back: Product operation, product revision and product transition; revision covers maintainability, flexibility and testability.

front: List the eight product quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2011.
back: Functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability.

front: What was the software crisis?
back: The 1960s situation where projects were late, over budget, unreliable and hard to maintain; the 1968 NATO conference proposed software engineering as the remedy.

front: What is the difference between procedural abstraction and data abstraction?
back: Procedural abstraction names a sequence of instructions with one function (e.g. open door) while hiding its steps; data abstraction names a collection of data that describes an object (e.g. door with its attributes).

front: Define fan-in and fan-out of a module.
back: Fan-in is the number of modules that directly call the module; fan-out is the number of modules it directly calls. Designers aim for high fan-in of utilities and limited fan-out.

front: What does the heuristic 'keep scope of effect within scope of control' mean?
back: Every module affected by a decision made in a module should lie in the subtree of modules that the deciding module controls, so decisions do not have side effects elsewhere.

front: Why does total cost versus number of modules form a U-shaped curve?
back: More modules lower the cost of building each one but raise interface and integration cost, so total cost is minimum at a moderate degree of modularity.

front: Which integration strategy needs drivers, and which needs stubs?
back: Bottom-up integration needs drivers to call the low-level clusters; top-down integration needs stubs to stand in for lower modules not yet integrated. Sandwich needs both.

front: What is the difference between load testing and stress testing?
back: Load testing checks behaviour at the expected peak workload; stress testing pushes the system beyond its designed limits to see how and where it fails.

front: Name the three kinds of interface error Sommerville identifies in component testing.
back: Interface misuse (wrong parameters), interface misunderstanding (wrong assumptions about behaviour) and timing errors (producer and consumer at different speeds).

front: Name the four pillars of OOP (APIE).
back: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance and Encapsulation.

front: What are the three models of Rumbaugh's OMT?
back: Object model (static structure, class diagrams), dynamic model (states and events, state diagrams) and functional model (value transformations, DFDs).

front: List the four Unified Process phases in order.
back: Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition; the architecture is stabilised during Elaboration.

front: How does run-time polymorphism differ from compile-time polymorphism?
back: Run-time polymorphism uses overriding and dynamic binding on the object's actual type; compile-time polymorphism uses overloading resolved by the compiler from argument types.

front: What is the difference between an essential and a real use case?
back: An essential use case is abstract and technology-free, recording only intentions and responsibilities; a real use case describes the interaction in terms of a concrete UI and hardware design.

front: What does a system sequence diagram show?
back: For one use-case scenario, the external actors, the system as a single black box, and the ordered system events (with parameters) crossing the system boundary.

front: What kinds of postconditions does an operation contract state?
back: Instance creation or deletion, attribute modification, and association formation or breaking among domain objects.

front: What is model-view separation?
back: Domain (model) objects must not directly know or call UI (view) objects; the UI depends on the domain layer, keeping business logic reusable and testable.

front: In what order should classes be implemented from a design model?
back: From least-coupled to most-coupled, so each class can be tested against already-working collaborators.

front: What is refactoring?
back: Restructuring existing code in small, test-verified steps to improve its internal design without changing its external behaviour.

front: Which design artefacts supply a method's signature and its body?
back: The signature comes from the design class diagram; the body is derived from the messages in the interaction diagrams.

front: What does Larman's implementation model contain?
back: All implementation artefacts: source and test code, database definitions, web/XML pages and configuration files.

front: What does PEAS stand for?
back: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors; it specifies an agent's task environment.

front: What is the difference between the agent function and the agent program?
back: The agent function is an abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions; the agent program is the concrete code that implements it on an architecture, taking the current percept as input.

front: On what four things does rationality depend?
back: The performance measure, the agent's prior knowledge of the environment, the actions available to it, and its percept sequence to date.

front: When is an agent called autonomous?
back: When its behaviour is determined by its own experience and learning rather than relying only on the designer's built-in knowledge.

front: Why does a simple reflex agent need a fully observable environment?
back: It decides only from the current percept with condition-action rules and keeps no memory, so it acts correctly only if the current percept reveals everything relevant.

front: What two kinds of knowledge make up the world model of a model-based agent?
back: How the world evolves independently of the agent, and how the agent's own actions change the world.

front: What advantage does a utility-based agent have over a goal-based agent?
back: Its utility function gives degrees of desirability, so it can trade off conflicting goals and weigh probability of success rather than only distinguishing goal from non-goal states.

front: Name the four components of a learning agent.
back: Performance element, critic, learning element and problem generator.

front: What is a semi-dynamic environment? Give an example.
back: One in which the environment does not change with time but the agent's performance score does; chess played with a clock.

front: How is taxi driving classified on all six main environment dimensions?
back: Partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic and continuous.

front: Distinguish episodic from sequential environments.
back: In an episodic environment each episode's action does not affect later episodes; in a sequential environment the current decision can affect all future decisions.

front: How many states does the two-square vacuum world have?
back: 8: two agent locations times four clean/dirty combinations of the squares (2 × 2^2).

front: What three sets define a constraint satisfaction problem?
back: A set of variables, a domain of possible values for each variable, and a set of constraints on allowed value combinations.

front: What does the least-constraining-value heuristic do?
back: It orders a variable's values so the value that rules out the fewest options for neighbouring variables is tried first.

front: How does forward checking work?
back: After each assignment it removes inconsistent values from the domains of unassigned neighbours and backtracks immediately if any domain becomes empty.

front: When is the arc X -> Y consistent?
back: When every value in the domain of X has at least one value in the domain of Y that satisfies the constraint between them.

front: Which uninformed search is optimal for arbitrary non-negative step costs?
back: Uniform-cost search, which always expands the frontier node with the lowest path cost g(n).

front: When is depth-limited search incomplete?
back: When the depth limit l is less than the depth d of the shallowest goal, because the goal is never reached.

front: What two conditions does bidirectional search need?
back: An explicit goal state to search back from, and the ability to compute predecessors (reversible actions).

front: What is the space complexity of iterative deepening search?
back: O(bd), linear in the solution depth, like depth-first search.

front: Why is greedy best-first search not optimal?
back: It expands by h(n) only and ignores the path cost g(n) already incurred, so it can commit to a path that looks close but is expensive.

front: For the 8-puzzle, which heuristic dominates: misplaced tiles or Manhattan distance?
back: Manhattan distance h2 dominates misplaced tiles h1 because h2 >= h1 for every state, and both are admissible, so A* with h2 expands fewer nodes.

front: Name the three landscape features that trap hill climbing.
back: Local maxima, plateaux (flat regions or shoulders) and ridges.

front: What does the temperature T control in simulated annealing?
back: The probability of accepting worse moves: high T accepts them often to escape local maxima, and as T is lowered the search behaves like hill climbing.

front: What do alpha and beta represent in alpha-beta pruning?
back: Alpha is the best value found so far for MAX along the current path; beta is the best (lowest) value found so far for MIN.

front: What is the horizon effect?
back: A depth-limited search wrongly judges a position because an unavoidable bad event is pushed just beyond the search depth; quiescence search reduces it.

front: Which components define a game for adversarial search?
back: Initial state, PLAYER, ACTIONS, RESULT, TERMINAL-TEST and UTILITY.

front: What is the effective branching factor of alpha-beta with perfect move ordering?
back: About sqrt(b), giving O(b^(m/2)) time instead of O(b^m).

front: When is P → Q false?
back: Only when P is true and Q is false; in every other row it is true.

front: What is the difference between a valid and a satisfiable sentence?
back: A valid sentence (tautology) is true in every interpretation; a satisfiable sentence is true in at least one.

front: List the steps to convert a propositional sentence to CNF.
back: Eliminate ↔, eliminate →, move ¬ inwards with De Morgan and double negation, then distribute ∨ over ∧.

front: What does deriving the empty clause mean in resolution refutation?
back: KB plus the negated goal is unsatisfiable, so the goal is entailed by the KB.

front: Translate 'Some student is clever' into FOPL.
back: ∃x (Student(x) ∧ Clever(x)); the existential pairs with ∧, not with →.

front: What is the MGU of Knows(John, x) and Knows(y, Mother(y))?
back: {y/John, x/Mother(John)}.

front: What restriction applies to existential instantiation?
back: The existential variable must be replaced by a brand-new constant (Skolem constant) that appears nowhere else in the KB.

front: What is the occurs check in unification?
back: A variable cannot be bound to a term containing that variable, so P(x) and P(F(x)) do not unify.

front: Name the four terms in Bayes' rule.
back: P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(B) the evidence or normaliser, and P(A|B) the posterior.

front: How many independent numbers does a Boolean node with 3 Boolean parents need in its CPT?
back: 2^3 = 8, one probability of true for each combination of parent values.

front: What is explaining away?
back: In a common-effect structure A → C ← B, observing C makes A and B dependent, so confirming one cause lowers belief in the other.

front: What conditional independence does every Bayesian network node satisfy?
back: Each node is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents.

front: What is the difference between NLU and NLG?
back: NLU maps text or speech to an internal meaning representation; NLG maps an internal meaning or data to natural-language text or speech.

front: Which NLP step interprets "Can you pass the salt?" as a request?
back: Pragmatic analysis, which reinterprets the literal meaning according to context and the speaker's intention.

front: What is a morpheme? Give free and bound examples.
back: The smallest meaningful unit of language; "happy" is a free morpheme and the affixes "un-" and "-ness" are bound morphemes.

front: What is a corpus in NLP?
back: A large structured collection of written or spoken texts, such as the Brown Corpus or Penn Treebank, used to train and evaluate language models.

front: What is an end effector? Give two examples.
back: The device at the end of a robot arm that interacts with the work, such as a gripper or a welding torch.

front: Why does a general-purpose manipulator need six degrees of freedom?
back: Three DOF fix the position (x, y, z) and three fix the orientation (roll, pitch, yaw) of the end effector in 3D space.

front: What happens in the preprocessing stage of machine vision?
back: The raw image is improved by removing noise, enhancing contrast and correcting distortion, e.g. with median filters or histogram equalisation.

front: State Asimov's First Law of Robotics.
back: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.

front: How does ID3 choose the attribute at each node?
back: It computes the information gain of every remaining attribute on the current examples and splits on the one with the highest gain, greedily and without backtracking.

front: What is the entropy of the PlayTennis set with 9 Yes and 5 No?
Why does C4.5 use gain ratio instead of plain information gain?
back: Information gain is biased towards attributes with many values (such as an ID); dividing by split information penalises such attributes.

front: What is reduced-error pruning?
back: Replacing a subtree by a leaf with its majority class whenever doing so does not lower accuracy on a separate validation set.

front: What independence assumption does naive Bayes make?
back: All features are conditionally independent of one another given the class, so P(x_1..x_n | c) = Π P(x_i | c).

front: What problem does Laplace smoothing solve?
back: The zero-frequency problem: a feature value unseen with a class would give probability 0 and wipe out the whole product; adding 1 to counts prevents this.

front: Why do naive Bayes implementations sum log probabilities?
back: Multiplying many probabilities smaller than 1 causes floating-point underflow; summing logs gives the same argmax safely.

front: What is the main difference between Mamdani and Sugeno inference?
back: Mamdani rule consequents are fuzzy sets that are aggregated and defuzzified; Sugeno consequents are crisp functions (linear or constant) combined by a weighted average.

front: List the steps of a fuzzy inference system.
back: Fuzzification, rule evaluation (with implication), aggregation of rule outputs, and defuzzification.

front: If μ_Tall(x) = 0.8, what is μ for 'very tall' and 'somewhat tall'?
back: Very tall = 0.8² = 0.64 (concentration); somewhat tall = √0.8 ≈ 0.89 (dilation).

front: What is elitism in a genetic algorithm?
back: Copying the best chromosome(s) of the current generation unchanged into the next, so the best solution found is never lost.

front: Why is rank selection sometimes preferred to roulette-wheel selection?
back: It uses ranks instead of raw fitness, so one very fit individual cannot dominate early (premature convergence) and pressure remains when fitnesses are close.

front: Which encoding suits the travelling salesman problem?
back: Permutation encoding, where each chromosome is an ordering of cities, used with order/PMX crossover and swap or inversion mutation.

front: Name four common GA termination conditions.
back: Maximum generations reached, target fitness achieved, no improvement for several generations, or time/evaluation budget exhausted.

front: Why must hidden layers use a non-linear activation function?
back: Stacking linear layers gives just another linear function, so without non-linearity a multilayer network could not model non-linear boundaries such as XOR.

front: What is the maximum value of the sigmoid derivative, and where does it occur?
Which activation is used in the output layer for multi-class classification?
back: Softmax, because it produces positive outputs that sum to 1 and can be read as class probabilities.

front: What distinguishes a recurrent network from a feedforward one?
back: A recurrent network has at least one feedback loop so outputs are fed back as inputs; a feedforward network has no cycles.

front: What does the perceptron convergence theorem state?
back: If the training data are linearly separable, the perceptron learning rule finds a separating weight vector in a finite number of steps.

front: Why can a single perceptron not learn XOR?
back: XOR is not linearly separable; no single line (hyperplane) separates the inputs with output 1 from those with output 0.

front: How do batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent differ?
back: Batch updates after the whole training set, stochastic after every single example, and mini-batch after each small group of examples.

front: What is the key difference between the perceptron rule and the delta rule?
back: The perceptron rule uses the error of the thresholded output; the delta rule uses the error of the continuous output and follows the gradient of squared error.

front: State Hebb's postulate in one line.
back: When two connected neurons are active together, the strength of the connection between them increases: neurons that fire together wire together.

front: Why is bipolar representation preferred for training a Hebb net?
back: With binary 0/1 data, any pair with x = 0 or t = 0 produces no weight change, so the net cannot learn from those cases; bipolar ±1 values always update.

front: What error does Adaline use during training?
back: The difference between the target and the linear net input (t − net), measured before the output quantiser.

front: What is Madaline?
back: A network of many Adaline units feeding a fixed logic unit (such as majority or AND), able to form non-linear regions and solve XOR.

front: What are the two passes of backpropagation?
back: A forward pass that computes all neuron outputs and the error, and a backward pass that propagates deltas from output to input layers to update weights.

front: How does a hidden layer let an MLP solve XOR?
back: Hidden units (e.g. OR and NAND) re-map the inputs into a space where the two classes become linearly separable, and the output unit (AND) combines them.

front: What does the momentum term do in backpropagation?
back: It adds a fraction α of the previous weight change, speeding progress in consistent directions, damping oscillations and helping escape shallow local minima.

front: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
back: In deep networks with saturating activations like sigmoid (derivative ≤ 0.25), deltas shrink layer by layer so early layers learn very slowly.

front: What two conditions on the weights define a Hopfield network?
back: Symmetric weights (w_ij = w_ji) and no self-connections (w_ii = 0).

front: Why does a Hopfield network always converge under asynchronous updates?
back: With symmetric weights and zero diagonal, each single-neuron update can only decrease or keep the energy, and the energy is bounded below, so a stable state is reached.

front: What is pattern completion in a Hopfield network?
back: Given a noisy or partial probe, the network evolves to the nearest stored pattern, acting as a content-addressable (associative) memory.

front: What are spurious states?
back: Stable states that were not stored, such as the complement −s of a stored pattern or mixtures of stored patterns.

front: When is A* search optimal?
back: With an admissible heuristic for tree search, or a consistent heuristic for graph search.

front: What is the space complexity of iterative deepening search?
back: O(bd), linear like DFS, while keeping BFS's completeness and optimality for unit step costs.

front: What are the fuzzy AND, OR and NOT operators?
back: AND is the minimum, OR is the maximum and NOT is 1 minus the membership value.

front: What is the derivative of the sigmoid function in terms of its output?
back: σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)), which is at most 0.25 (at x = 0).

front: Name the four approaches to defining AI.
back: Thinking humanly (cognitive modelling), acting humanly (Turing test), thinking rationally (laws of thought) and acting rationally (rational agents).

front: What does the total Turing test require beyond the standard test?
back: Computer vision to perceive objects and robotics to manipulate objects and move, in addition to NLP, knowledge representation, reasoning and learning.

front: Distinguish strong AI from weak AI.
back: Weak AI claims machines can act as if intelligent; strong AI claims a suitably programmed machine actually has a mind and genuinely thinks.

front: Which discipline gave AI utility, decision theory and game theory?
back: Economics, which studies how to make decisions that maximise payoff, including under uncertainty and against other agents.

front: What are the five components of a well-defined search problem?
back: Initial state, actions, transition model RESULT(s, a), goal test and path-cost function.

front: What is the difference between the frontier and the explored set?
back: The frontier (open list) holds generated nodes not yet expanded; the explored set (closed list) holds states already expanded so graph search does not revisit them.

front: What do b, d and m denote in search complexity analysis?
back: b is the branching factor, d the depth of the shallowest goal, and m the maximum depth of any path in the state space.

front: Give one toy problem and one real-world problem that are formulated as state-space search.
back: Toy: 8-puzzle, water jug, missionaries and cannibals, 8-queens. Real-world: route finding, travelling salesperson, VLSI layout, robot navigation.

front: Name the four properties of a good knowledge representation system.
back: Representational adequacy, inferential adequacy, inferential efficiency and acquisitional efficiency.

front: What is the difference between an instance link and an IS-A link?
back: instance connects an individual object to its class, while IS-A connects a subclass to its superclass; both support property inheritance.

front: What are demons in a frame system?
back: Attached procedures such as if-needed (run when an empty slot is read) and if-added (run when a value is stored) that fire automatically.

front: What does a script represent, and who proposed it?
back: A stereotyped sequence of events in a context, such as a restaurant visit, with props, roles, entry conditions, scenes and results; proposed by Schank and Abelson.

front: What is the role of working memory in an expert system?
back: It holds the facts of the current case: data entered by the user and the intermediate conclusions derived by the inference engine during the consultation.

front: What is an expert system shell? Give an example.
back: An expert system with its domain knowledge removed, providing the inference engine, interface and explanation facility so only rules need to be added; EMYCIN and CLIPS are examples.

front: Distinguish declarative and procedural knowledge.
back: Declarative knowledge is knowing what (facts and relations, e.g. Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal); procedural knowledge is knowing how (steps and methods, e.g. how to change a tyre).

front: Why is knowledge acquisition called the bottleneck of expert-system development?
back: Expert knowledge is tacit and heuristic, hard for experts to articulate and slow for the knowledge engineer to elicit, encode and validate.

front: State Mitchell's definition of machine learning.
back: A program learns from experience E with respect to tasks T and performance measure P if its performance at T, measured by P, improves with E.

front: What are the four components of a learning agent?
back: Performance element (chooses actions), critic (gives feedback against a standard), learning element (makes improvements) and problem generator (suggests exploratory actions).

front: Classification vs regression?
back: Both are supervised; classification predicts a discrete class label, regression predicts a continuous numeric value.

front: What is a policy in reinforcement learning?
back: A mapping π from states to actions; the agent learns the policy that maximises expected cumulative (discounted) reward.

front: Which part of a biological neuron corresponds to the weight in an ANN?
back: The synapse; its strength determines how much an incoming signal influences the receiving neuron, just as a weight does.

front: What are the weights and threshold of a 2-input McCulloch–Pitts AND gate?
back: w1 = w2 = 1 with threshold θ = 2, so the unit fires only when both inputs are 1.

front: What does the bias do in the neuron model y = f(w · x + b)?
back: It shifts the decision boundary away from the origin and acts like a negative threshold (b = −θ).

front: Name three key differences between biological and artificial neural networks.
back: Biological neurons switch in milliseconds but are massively parallel with about 10^11 units; artificial units switch in nanoseconds, are far fewer and learn by explicit algorithms.
